 When I told my parents that I planned to travel to Harare, they were not too excited and sent me quite a few
 articles about why I should not travel to Zimbabwe. For example, both the Swedish and Finish embassies warn
 against traveling there due to political unrest, demonstrations, and different diseases (AIDS, malaria, hepatitis A
 and B, etc). However, when traveling around Zimbabwe and walking around in Harare, mostly alone, I actually
 felt quite safe. This was also the opinion of other White people who are living there (mostly diplomats or people
 working at NGOs) to whom I spoke. Obviously, I was not out after the sundown; I did not take photos of
 Mugabe's policemen, and, of course, I was cautious. Nevertheless, I was surprised at how safe I felt: indeed, in
 contrast to everything I had read.

  The people living in Zimbabwe are extremely kind and helpful; many people who have visited the county claim
  that people there are the kindest people in the world. Obviously, hard to know — but all the people I met were
  extremely kind, helpful, warmhearted, and polite.

 In comparison to other African countries, Zimbabwe has an extremely well developed educational system.
 Zimbabwe has the highest adult literacy rate in Africa — around 90%. Parents — from upper, middle, or lower
 class families — take great pride in sending their children to school or teaching their children themselves.
 Furthermore, the educational system in Zimbabwe is recognized as being one of the best in Africa. It is so well
 recognized (I was told) that parents from neighboring countries want to send their children to school there. What
 is different about the school system from those in other African countries (for example in Tanzania and
 Mozambique) is that it encourages students to reflect, i.e., children do not only learn A and B and C by rote, they
 also learn why things are as they are and what can be made of them. This, in short, means that Zimbabwe
 possesses substantially great human capital than other developing countries. I find this to be very interesting. It's
 also worth mentioning that almost everyone — whether old or young — speaks two languages; English and Shona
 or Ndebele (the languages of Zimbabwe's two major ethnic groups).

 Zimbabwe's natural beauty, flora, and fauna are fantastic! During my trip in Zimbabwe I had the pleasure of
 seeing giraffes, zebras, rhinos, different kinds of birds, and antelopes among other animals. The landscape — with
 plains, big rocks, fields, forests, and savannahs — is just stunning. Until 2007 tourism in Zimbabwe was growing.
 However, since then, it has steadily declined. I saw NO tourists at all, and the two tourist offices that exist in
 Harare were closed. Tourism in Zimbabwe consists mostly of visiting Victoria Falls, I was told. Around 2000 it
 was fairly easy to travel to Zimbabwe; however, today, most airline companies have pulled out of the country.
 The last direct flight from Europe stopped flying just a few months ago. This, I believe, is extremely sad —
 Zimbabwe offers tremendous beauty.

  When walking around Harare or driving on roads outside the city, it is clear that the economy in Zimbabwe has
  declined dramatically since 2007. The street lights that once worked do not work anywhere; the roads are getting
  worse and worse; and greenhouses that were once in use are not in service anymore and stand empty. You see



                                                                                                          EFTA01001153
 this everywhere. It is hard to believe that only 7 or 8 years ago all these things were fully functioning. This made
me sad. It was as if I were walking around in the shadows of what was once a blooming country. Thinking about
the great natural resources and the large human capital the country possesses makes it even sadder.

It is hard not to mention the poverty there; everywhere people try to sell whatever they can find (sculptures,
food, maize, wood, tomatoes, stones, plastic bags, anything and everything). Begging children and parents are
everywhere. However, despite this misery; there seems to be hope and love: I truly admire this. Before 2007
Zimbabwe had a quite large middle class. However, since then most of the middle class has fallen into the lower
class, and inequality has increased substantially. Scarcity of water and electricity is obvious. Restrooms at
restaurants, hotels, the airport had no hot water and the place where I stayed lost its electricity a couple of hours
every day. This is, naturally, a particular problem for hospitals

Zimbabwe has been called the bread basket of Africa. Its soil and climate are very well suited for crops such as
corn, tobacco, maize, and even bananas. I spoke with quite a few White investors and White farmers who
invested substantially in farms around Zimbabwe and have reaped the rewards of doing so. For example, I spoke
with a man working at a company that owns a large banana farm; he clamed that since the climate there is less
humid than the climate in, for example, central America, farmers in Zimbabwe do not have the same problems
with diseases. The investors I spoke with argued that, even though the economic climate in Zimbabwe is
worsening, the benefits from investing there is higher compared to investing in, for example, Tanzania (where
the economy is growing), due to the school system (which as I mentioned before, focuses on self-reflection,
which leads to better entrepreneurship and business practices) as well as Zimbabwe's large natural resources.

The political climate is hot in Zimbabwe right now. The 1st of December there are elections for vice president.
Every newspaper is writing about it. The contest is mostly between two women and one man. One of the women
is Mugabe's wife. According to diplomats I spoke with, it will be a disaster if she wins vice presidency, as most
people have no respect for her. Mugabe is 92 years old; he will most likely not live another five years, which
means that the one appointed vice president the 1st of December might become Zimbabwe's next president —
which indeed will be important for the future of Zimbabwe.

people watch TV, have cell phones, and use computers. Multiple stores in Harare wanted their customers to look
them up at Facebook. Maybe there will be great gains for companies such as Ericsson, Microsoft, and others in
Zimbabwe a few years from now.
